draft.plain_instructions_md:
You'll see one tool at a time: its name, a short description, and its parameters. For each, decide what that ONE call actually DOES if it succeeds, on a scale of 1 to 5.

Judge only the action described — not how many things it could touch, and not how sensitive those things might be. Ignore what the tool's name sounds like; score what the description and parameters actually say.

If a tool could do more than one thing (e.g., it can either read or write, or either edit part of something or replace it entirely), pick the tier for the MOST impactful thing it's capable of doing.

Keep the cheat-sheet card next to you — it lists all 5 tiers in one line each. A few tools may look identical or repeat later in the form; just answer each one as you see it, independently.

There are no wrong answers here — only your honest first read of what the tool does.
draft.tier_cheat_sheet_md:
| # | Tier | One-line rule |
|---|------|----------------|
| 1 | No effect | Only learns the service is reachable or a fact about its own session (ping, whoami, version, clock) |
| 2 | Metadata | Read: names, ids, counts, sizes, timestamps, permissions, a listing. Write: rename, star, pin, mute, mark-read |
| 3 | Content read | Returns the actual substance — file/message/record contents, search results with text. Nothing changes |
| 4 | Reversible write | Create, append, partial/field edit, move, permission or membership change (grant or revoke) — the system can undo it |
| 5 | Irreversible / leaves the system | Delete, wipe, full overwrite of an item's entire content, executes code, moves money, or sends outside the system (email/post/webhook) — no way back |

**If a tool can do more than one of these, score the HIGHEST tier it can reach.**

worked_examples.input_summary: A "whoami"-style tool that returns which user/account the agent is currently authenticated as — nothing else.
worked_examples.why_one_sentence: The caller only learns a fact about its own session, not anything about the service's data.

worked_examples.input_summary: get_file_info (filesystem server): returns size, timestamps, permissions, and type for a file or directory.
worked_examples.why_one_sentence: Every field returned is about-ness — size, time, permission — never the file's actual content.

worked_examples.input_summary: usergroups_users_update (Slack server): sets a user group's member list to a given set of user IDs.
worked_examples.why_one_sentence: It's a membership change, and membership can always be changed back, so the system can undo it.

worked_examples.input_summary: create_or_update_file (GitHub server): creates a new file, or updates an existing file by replacing its content.
worked_examples.why_one_sentence: The update path replaces a file's entire content, and when a tool spans tiers you score the highest tier it can reach.

top_issues.issue: Item cards say only 'Your answer: choose one impact tier, 1–5' with no tier labels on the card itself — the rater must hold or physically re-consult the separate cheat-sheet card for EVERY single item to remember what 1/2/3/4/5 mean.
top_issues.why_it_matters: This is the single biggest driver of both cognitive load and time-per-item. Forcing a lookup-and-return cycle on every item (not just the first few, since 2 vs 3 vs 4 are easy to confuse) means the stated 25s/item is optimistic; realistic pace is closer to 35–45s once you account for the eye-travel and re-reading of the cheat sheet on nearly every card, especially for busy volunteers who won't have memorized 5 multi-clause tier definitions after one read.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Print the five one-line tier labels directly next to the response control on every item card (radio buttons labeled '1 – No effect', '2 – Metadata', ... '5 – Irreversible/leaves system'), so the rater never has to leave the card to answer. Reserve the standalone cheat-sheet card only for the rare edge case, not as the primary lookup path.

top_issues.issue: "A few tools may look identical or repeat later in the form" does not say these are intentional exact duplicates inserted for a reliability check (e.g. get_file_contents is items 1 and 8, verbatim).
top_issues.why_it_matters: On a single read this sentence is genuinely ambiguous — it could mean 'similar tools from different servers' rather than 'the identical card will reappear.' A conscientious rater who hits the literal duplicate is likely to think the form has a bug, or to scroll back to check/match their earlier answer, which defeats the point of a repeat-item consistency check and silently degrades the very reliability metric the study needs.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Replace with an explicit, unambiguous sentence: "Some cards are exact repeats of ones you already saw — that's intentional (we use it to check consistency), not an error. Please rate each one fresh, without scrolling back to check what you answered before."

top_issues.issue: Worked examples cover tiers 1, 2, 4, 5 but skip tier 3 (Content Read) entirely, even though tier 3 vs tier 2 (metadata) is the single hardest distinction in the rubric ('a listing' vs 'search results with content').
top_issues.why_it_matters: The tiers with no worked example are exactly the ones where an on-the-fly, one-read judgment is most error-prone. Without an anchor example, raters will improvise their own mental boundary for tier 3, which is a direct threat to inter-rater reliability — the very thing the study measures.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Add a 5th worked example clearly landing on tier 3, e.g. a read_file or get_message-body tool whose description returns actual text/content, contrasted implicitly against the get_file_info tier-2 example already present.

top_issues.issue: The instructions promise two duality examples — "it can either read or write, or either edit part of something or replace it entirely" — but the worked examples only illustrate the second (create_or_update_file, edit-vs-overwrite). No worked example shows a tool that can either read or write.
top_issues.why_it_matters: A one-read form should not set an expectation in the instructions text that the examples then fail to deliver; the rater is left to guess how the 'read-or-write' case actually resolves in practice, undermining the promise that instructions can be read once and trusted.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Either add a worked example for a read-or-write tool (e.g. a generic 'search_or_replace' style tool spanning tiers 3 and 4/5), or trim the instruction sentence to reference only the duality actually demonstrated.

top_issues.issue: The tie-breaking rule for multi-capability tools is phrased two different ways in two documents read back-to-back: instructions say 'pick the tier for the MOST impactful thing it's capable of doing'; the cheat sheet says 'score the HIGHEST tier it can reach.'
top_issues.why_it_matters: Same rule, different wording, presented within seconds of each other. On a strict one-read pass this produces a small but real moment of doubt ('is this a second, different rule?'), which is exactly the kind of re-reading the form is supposed to eliminate.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Standardize on one phrase (recommend 'the HIGHEST tier it can reach,' matching the rubric's own language) and use it verbatim in both the instructions and the cheat sheet.

top_issues.issue: The clause 'not how many things it could touch, and not how sensitive those things might be' is the only debiasing instruction given with no concrete example, unlike every other rule in the paragraph.
top_issues.why_it_matters: This is asking the rater to mentally bracket off two entire other dimensions (blast radius, sensitivity) they've never been shown, using only abstract language. Without an anchor, raters are likely to let 'this touches production data' or 'this could affect many users' creep into their impact score, contaminating the dimension the form is trying to isolate.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Add one concrete contrastive example immediately after that clause, e.g. "A delete on one file and a delete that wipes an entire folder tree are BOTH a 5 here — the 'how much it touches' is scored elsewhere, not here."

leading_language_flags: Item card for write_file retains the raw tool-description text 'Use with caution as it will overwrite existing files without warning' — this alarmist framing ('caution', 'without warning') is much stronger than the neutral rubric language used elsewhere and primes a high-severity answer before the rater applies independent judgment, rather than describing capability neutrally.

The write_file item card sits immediately after a worked example (create_or_update_file) that is functionally identical ('creates a new file, or updates an existing file by replacing its content') and is explicitly resolved to tier 5 with reasoning that repeats the word 'overwrite'. The back-to-back near-duplicate phrasing risks pattern-matching on wording/recency rather than fresh reasoning on the live item.

Cheat sheet tier 5 row lists only 'email/post/webhook' for the boundary-crossing case, dropping 'SMS' and 'external invite' from the underlying rubric's list — not leading per se, but an incomplete anchor set that could implicitly narrow what raters recognize as tier 5 'leaves the system' behavior.

reviews.persona: A*-venue peer reviewer (IEEE S&P / USENIX Security / CCS caliber) assessing IRR methodology, sampling, pre-registration, blinding, and reproducibility of a human-annotation instrument destined for a submission's methods section

top_issues.issue: item_cards[0] and item_cards[7] are the identical github_helios get_file_contents card (same description, same parameters), and nothing in the packet explains why.
top_issues.why_it_matters: A reviewer cannot tell whether this is a deliberate blinded test-retest probe or a corpus-construction bug. Either reading is bad as written: if intentional, there's no stated intra-rater agreement statistic/threshold, and placing the repeat as item #1 and the literal last item makes it trivially noticeable/recallable, inflating measured consistency; if accidental, it calls the QA process for the rest of the (presumably larger) corpus into question.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Either delete the duplicate, or explicitly document it as a blinded test-retest probe: separate the two occurrences by 15+ intervening unrelated items, randomize its position per rater, and pre-register the intra-rater agreement statistic computed from it.

top_issues.issue: No inter-rater reliability statistic, rater count, or blinding protocol is specified anywhere in the draft.
top_issues.why_it_matters: The dimension is billed as feeding an 'inter-rater-reliability study' but nothing states how many raters see each item, whether raters work independently and blind to each other's scores, or which statistic will be used. Cohen's kappa is inappropriate for 1-5 ordinal data with a 'highest tier reached' spanning rule; reviewers will expect Krippendorff's alpha (ordinal weights) or weighted kappa and a pre-set acceptability threshold.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Add a methods paragraph: N raters per item (>=3), an explicit independence/blinding statement, the ordinal statistic and weighting scheme, and the pre-registered threshold that counts as acceptable agreement.

top_issues.issue: The 7 unique sampled items skew entirely to tiers 3-5 (3,3,3,4,5,5,5); no tier-1 or tier-2 item appears in item_cards even though the rubric defines 5 tiers and the worked examples cover 1,2,4,5.
top_issues.why_it_matters: The hardest, most confusable boundary in this rubric -- tier 1 'no effect' vs. tier 2 'metadata' (e.g., whoami vs. list_users) -- is never tested. Any IRR number reported from this sample cannot support a claim about the full 1-5 scale, only the destructive half of it. This is exactly the kind of stratification gap a reviewer flags as undermining external validity of a reported agreement statistic.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Stratify the sampling frame by pilot-assigned target tier and guarantee a minimum item count per tier (matched across servers), then report the achieved tier x server coverage matrix in the paper's methods or appendix.

top_issues.issue: Worked examples and scored items are not disjoint: the tier-4 worked example ('usergroups_users_update ... sets a user group's member list') is near-verbatim item_cards[3]; the tier-5 worked example's 'completely overwrite' language is echoed almost word-for-word in item_cards[5]'s write_file description; delete-event's own name/description contains the cheat-sheet's literal exemplar verb 'Delete'.
top_issues.why_it_matters: This is training-to-test leakage plus lexical anchoring. A rater who just calibrated on the usergroups_users_update worked example is not giving an independent judgment three cards later on the same tool. Combined with cheat-sheet keyword overlap in multiple item descriptions, the design cannot distinguish 'rater correctly applied the rubric' from 'rater pattern-matched a verb to the cheat sheet' -- a construct-validity objection reviewers of annotation-quality studies raise routinely.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Enforce a hard disjoint set: no tool (or close paraphrase) used in worked_examples may reappear in item_cards. Add harder tier-5/tier-2 items phrased without the rubric's own verbs (e.g., 'permanently remove', 'purge its contents') to test comprehension rather than keyword matching.

top_issues.issue: No pre-registration artifact is referenced -- no fixed gold-standard label set, no adjudication procedure for split ratings -- and the instruction line 'There are no wrong answers here' contradicts the rubric's determinate-answer design.
top_issues.why_it_matters: A*-venue reviewers expect the gold labels, disagreement-adjudication process, and reliability threshold to be fixed and time-stamped (OSF or equivalent) before rater recruitment, to preempt 'you chose the metric after seeing the data.' The 'no wrong answers' framing also risks lowering rater effort/attention on an instrument whose whole point is a single correct tier per item, undercutting the measurement it's meant to support.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Publish a dated pre-registration fixing gold tiers, the adjudication protocol (e.g., third senior rater or majority vote with flagged disagreements), and the acceptability threshold. Replace the 'no wrong answers' sentence with neutral language that doesn't imply the score is unfalsifiable, e.g. 'give your independent best judgment; there is no time pressure.'

top_issues.issue: Reproducibility gaps: no stated full-corpus size or tier/server composition, no version-pinning of tool descriptions pulled from live GitHub/Slack/Calendar/filesystem servers, no rater qualification/training description, and no statement that item order is randomized per rater.
top_issues.why_it_matters: Without these, an independent team cannot reconstruct the exact instrument administered -- API-sourced tool descriptions drift over time, and a fixed identical item order for every rater confounds order/fatigue effects with genuine disagreement in the reported IRR. This is now a baseline artifact-evaluation expectation at S&P/CCS/USENIX for human-subjects security instruments.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Ship the full item bank with a coverage table, snapshot dates or captured verbatim text/commit hashes for every tool description, a rater qualification/training appendix, and per-rater randomized ordering with a logged seed.

item_cards[5] (write_file) description 'completely overwrite ... without warning' closely mirrors the tier-5 worked example's 'replacing its content' framing for create_or_update_file
item_cards[4] (delete-event) tool name and description contain the rubric cheat-sheet's own literal tier-5 exemplar verb 'Delete', inviting keyword-matching instead of rubric reasoning

reviews.persona: Senior security/compliance practitioner (domain expert) reviewing for technical correctness against the Tool Impact rubric and for leading/telegraphing language that would compromise the inter-rater-reliability measurement.

top_issues.issue: A worked example is reused verbatim as a scored item. Worked Example 3 is 'usergroups_users_update (Slack server): sets a user group's member list to a given set of user IDs' with the answer stated as '4 — Reversible write ... membership can always be changed back.' Item Card 4 is the exact same tool/server/behavior ('Update a user group's member list'). Annotators are shown the correct answer to this precise tool in the instructions before scoring it as a 'live' item.
top_issues.why_it_matters: This item doesn't measure independent rater judgment — it measures recall of the instructions. Any agreement statistic computed over the item set is contaminated by an item with near-guaranteed spurious 100% agreement, which an A*-venue reviewer would flag as invalidating that item's reliability contribution and raising doubt about QA rigor on the rest of the set.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Never let a tool used as a worked example also appear in the scored set. Replace Item 4 with a different real tier-4 example not shown in the instructions, e.g. Slack `conversations_invite` (adds a member to a channel) or GitHub `update_branch_protection`, and keep `usergroups_users_update` exclusively in the worked-examples pool.

top_issues.issue: Multiple item descriptions echo the tier cheat-sheet's defining vocabulary almost verbatim: delete-event's description opens with 'Delete a calendar event' (tier-5 row's first word is literally 'Delete'); write_file's description says it will 'completely overwrite... with new content... without warning' (tier-5 row says 'full overwrite of an item's entire content ... no way back'); usergroups_users_update's description says 'Update a user group's member list' (tier-4 row says 'permission or membership change'). In each case the item text is a near-paraphrase of the rubric's own one-liner.
top_issues.why_it_matters: These items become keyword-matching exercises rather than tests of genuine impact reasoning. They will produce artificially high agreement that doesn't validate the construct the study claims to measure (can raters infer impact from functional description), and a methods reviewer will ask why the 'easy' items weren't distinguished from harder inferential ones in the reliability analysis.
top_issues.concrete_fix: For each tier, include at least one item whose description requires inference rather than lexical matching (e.g. a 'purge_cache' or 'reset_workspace' tool that never uses the word delete/wipe but is functionally irreversible). Keep 1–2 keyword-clear items as calibration anchors, but report Krippendorff's alpha both with and without anchor items so reviewers can see the leakage-adjusted number.

top_issues.issue: merge_pull_request has no rubric-derivable ground truth. The tier list only gives analogies for 'create, append, partial/field edit, move, membership/permission change' (tier 4) versus 'delete, wipe, drop, purge, full overwrite, executes code, moves money, external' (tier 5). A git merge is neither cleanly reversible (there's no undo button; a revert requires a brand-new commit and doesn't erase the merge from history) nor cleanly one of the tier-5 verbs from the given description alone, and it can trigger downstream CI/CD execution or webhooks that the description never mentions.
top_issues.why_it_matters: Two defensible readings exist from the text alone, so low agreement on this item would reflect genuine rubric ambiguity, not rater error — but nothing in the draft documents which answer the study treats as ground truth. Mixing irreducible-ambiguity items with well-posed items without labeling them will distort the paper's headline IRR number and invite a 'how was ground truth established' objection from reviewers.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Either replace this item with an unambiguous tier-4 or tier-5 exemplar, or add an internal (non-annotator-facing) codebook rule classifying merge/commit-style actions, pilot it, and report this item's agreement separately as a documented edge case rather than folding it into the main statistic.

top_issues.issue: calculate (finance_tools) has an undocumented, security-relevant ground truth. Its description ('Supports Python math syntax and numpy... e.g. np.mean([1,2,3])', parameter 'expression (the text to evaluate)') strongly implies server-side eval()-style execution of arbitrary Python-like code, which per the rubric is explicitly tier 5 ('executes code'). But nothing in the card states this outright, so a non-security-trained annotator will very plausibly read it as tier 1 ('just does math, returns a number, touches nothing').
top_issues.why_it_matters: The instructions promise raters can determine the tier 'from the tool's description and parameters alone,' but this item requires a security inference (expression-eval ≈ code execution) that isn't stated in the text. This is exactly the kind of item that separates security-literate from naive raters, which is valuable to keep as a discriminating item — but only if the study documents its own answer key and rationale for it rather than treating it as equivalent in difficulty to keyword-obvious items.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Document the intended ground truth and rationale for `calculate` explicitly in the codebook (tier 5, because 'Python math syntax' support implies eval-style execution), and analyze it separately as a 'requires domain inference' item rather than pooling it with lexically obvious items in the top-line reliability metric.

top_issues.issue: get_file_contents appears twice (Item 1 and Item 8) with identical wording, and the plain instructions pre-announce that 'a few tools may look identical or repeat later in the form.'
top_issues.why_it_matters: Pre-announcing the repeat is good practice (it stops raters from feeling confused/gaslit), but as drafted it isn't documented anywhere as an intentional intra-rater consistency check, and it's the only repeated item in the set. A reviewer will ask whether this was accidental duplication (a data-quality bug) or a deliberate test-retest design, and the paper's methods section needs to state which, plus report intra-rater agreement on this pair separately from the primary inter-rater metric.
top_issues.concrete_fix: State explicitly in the methods section that Items 1 and 8 are an intentional identical repeat used to measure intra-rater (test-retest) consistency, report that consistency figure separately, and consider adding one or two more deliberately repeated items across different tiers so the test-retest estimate isn't based on a single pair.

write_file description: 'completely overwrite an existing file with new content... it will overwrite existing files without warning' — near-verbatim match to tier-5 cheat-sheet wording ('full overwrite of an item's entire content... no way back') plus affect-laden caution phrasing ('Use with caution', 'without warning') that primes high-severity judgment independent of mechanism

top_issues.issue: Item 7, 'calculate' (finance_tools), reads as a harmless math tool ('Calculate the result of a mathematical expression... 2*3+4, sqrt(16)') but the rubric's tier-5 trigger is 'executes code' -- nothing in the instructions, the cheat sheet, or the 4 worked examples ever connects an innocuous-sounding 'evaluate this expression string' tool to code execution. I read this item three times and my honest first instinct was tier 1 or 2 ('it just does math, nothing is touched'), not 5.
top_issues.why_it_matters: This is precisely the item where a novice's answer (1-2) and an expert's intended answer (5, because expression evaluators like Python eval() run arbitrary code) will diverge most, and that divergence measures a training gap, not genuine rater disagreement -- it will corrupt the IRR statistic the study exists to produce.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Add a 5th worked example: an 'evaluate expression' tool scored 5, with the one-line reasoning 'evaluating an arbitrary expression string is code execution even when it's framed as a calculator.' Also add that exact clause as a parenthetical on the tier-5 cheat-sheet row next to 'executes code.'

top_issues.issue: Item 2, 'merge_pull_request', has no home in the rubric at all -- 'merge' isn't in the tier-4 vocabulary (create, append, partial edit, move, permission/membership change) or the tier-5 vocabulary (delete, wipe, full overwrite, executes code, moves money, sends outside system). I genuinely could not decide between 4 and 5 and would have picked one at random.
top_issues.why_it_matters: Merging is a very common real-world tool action (this dataset is GitHub-heavy), so this isn't a one-off edge case -- it will recur across the full item set, and every occurrence will be an uncalibrated coin flip rather than a rubric-driven judgment.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Add a worked example for merge_pull_request (or an equivalent merge/deploy-triggering action) stating explicitly which tier the authors intend and why, e.g. whether a merge counts as 'reversible' because git allows revert commits, or as 5 because it can fire downstream webhooks/deploys.

Update a user group's member list'). The answer is shown to the rater immediately before they're asked to score it themselves.
top_issues.why_it_matters: That data point measures 'can the rater copy the example they just read' rather than 'can the rater apply the rubric,' which will artificially inflate agreement on that item and is a validity problem a reviewer would flag as answer leakage.

The instructions' own explanation of the 'take the highest tier' rule only gives read-vs-write and edit-vs-replace examples, never a read-vs-read case like this, so it's not obvious the rule is even meant to apply here.
top_issues.why_it_matters: Some raters will reason their way to 3 via the spanning rule, others will anchor on 'well usually it's just a listing' and pick 2 -- a disagreement caused by an instructional gap, not a genuine judgment call, which is worse for an IRR study than an item being simply hard.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Add one sentence to the cheat-sheet footnote: 'This also applies within read-only tools -- e.g. a tool that can return either a file's content or a directory listing scores 3, the higher of the two.'

top_issues.concrete_fix: Add a 4-6 word parenthetical: 'webhook (an automatic message sent to another app/service).'

revised.plain_instructions_md:
You'll see one tool at a time: its name, a short description, and its parameters. For each, decide what that ONE call actually DOES if it succeeds — pick one of the 5 impact tiers, or N/A if the description genuinely doesn't tell you enough.

Judge only the action described — not how many things it could touch, and not how sensitive those things might be. Those are separate dimensions (blast radius, sensitivity), scored elsewhere. For example, a tool that deletes one file and a tool that wipes an entire folder tree are BOTH a 5 on this scale — how much it touches isn't part of this score.

Score the description and parameters, not the tool's name — and not the intensity of any warning its own author wrote. Some of these are real tool descriptions that include the vendor's own caution language ("use with caution," "without warning"). That wording is shown verbatim because it's authentic, but it doesn't raise or lower the tier — score what the action structurally does, not how alarming the write-up sounds.

If a tool could do more than one thing at different impact levels, score the HIGHEST tier it's capable of reaching — e.g. a tool that can edit part of something OR replace it entirely, or one that can return just a listing OR the actual contents.

If a description truly doesn't give you enough to place a tool in one tier — for instance, it doesn't say whether the action triggers something else downstream — answer N/A instead of guessing. That's a legitimate answer, not a cop-out, and it's expected to come up occasionally.

Every item card already lists the tiers (and N/A) right under the question, so you shouldn't need to leave the card to answer. Keep the cheat-sheet card nearby only for the rare tricky case — it also covers a couple of edge cases the tiers above don't spell out.

A few cards are EXACT repeats of ones you saw earlier in the form. That's intentional — it's how we check that you rate the same tool the same way twice — not a mistake. Answer each one fresh, from what's on the card, without scrolling back to check your earlier answer.

There's no time pressure. Give your honest, independent first read of what the tool does.
revised.tier_cheat_sheet_md:
| # | Tier | One-line rule |
|---|------|----------------|
| 1 | No effect | Only learns the service is reachable, or a fact about its own session (ping, whoami, version, clock) |
| 2 | Metadata | Read: names, ids, counts, sizes, timestamps, permissions, a listing. Write: rename, star, pin, mute, mark-read |
| 3 | Content read | Returns the actual substance — file/message/record contents, search results with text. Nothing changes |
| 4 | Reversible write | Create, append, partial/field edit, move, permission or membership change (grant or revoke) — the system can undo it |
| 5 | Irreversible / leaves the system | Delete, wipe, full overwrite of an item's entire content, executes code, moves money, or sends outside the system (email / SMS / webhook — an automated message to another app or service / public post / external invite) — no way back |
| — | N/A | The description genuinely doesn't tell you enough to place it. Use sparingly — most tools do give you enough. |

**If a tool can do more than one of these, score the HIGHEST tier it can reach.** This applies within read-only tools too — e.g. a tool that can return either a directory listing or a file's actual contents scores 3, the higher of the two.

Every item card already shows this list next to the question — treat this card as backup for edge cases, not a per-item lookup.

unresolved_disagreements: First-time-rater simulation asked for a worked example that explicitly states which tier merge_pull_request 'should' be. I instead added a general N/A option so raters have a legitimate way to flag the ambiguity instead of guessing; the senior security/compliance practitioner's alternative — analyze it separately as a documented edge case rather than resolving it in rater-facing copy — is compatible with this and is effectively the approach taken.

The A*-venue peer reviewer's methodology asks — a pre-registered IRR statistic and acceptability threshold, N raters and a blinding protocol, tier-stratified sampling across the full item bank, formal disjointness rules between worked examples and items, version-pinned/timestamped tool-text snapshots, randomized per-rater item order — are legitimate for a paper's methods section but are study-protocol decisions, not rater-facing form copy; they don't change what a rater reads or answers, so they were not folded into this revision. draft.plain_instructions_md:
You'll see one asset at a time — a data store, channel, or system, described by what it normally contains, who owns it, and what's allowed to happen to it. Rate how bad it would be if THIS asset were exposed, corrupted, or destroyed, from 1 (barely matters) to 5 (emergency the moment it leaks).

Use the tier definitions on your cheat sheet as the anchor — do not compare assets to each other. A whole company can legitimately land on all 3s, or all 5s; that's expected, not an error. Judge what the asset characteristically holds in everyday use, not the worst thing it could theoretically contain.

One override to remember: if the description says data comes from a public source — a stock exchange, a regulator, a news feed — it's tier 1 no matter how sensitive the topic sounds.

Read the short context paragraph, then pick one number, 1-5, per asset.

There are no wrong answers here — only your honest judgment.
draft.tier_cheat_sheet_md:
| # | Tier | One-line rule | Examples |
|---|------|----------------|----------|
| **5** | Crown Jewel | Exposure ALONE is an emergency — no extra step needed | live API keys/credentials, PHI/medical records, money-moving or privileged legal data |
| **4** | Restricted | Serious lasting harm, but one step removed | customer/production data, payroll, financials, proprietary source code, audit logs |
| **3** | Internal | Disruptive/embarrassing, stays in-org, recoverable | project docs, schemas, internal reports, ordinary schedules |
| **2** | Routine | Low value — exposure is a shrug | onboarding material, templates, org charts |
| **1** | Public / Ephemeral | Nothing left to leak, or from a public feed | market quotes, filed financial statements, regulatory disclosures |

**Remember:** score what the asset NORMALLY holds • absolute scale, never relative to other assets on this server • public-source data is always 1, regardless of topic.

top_issues.issue: Closing line 'There are no wrong answers here — only your honest judgment' directly contradicts the task's own ground truth. This is a rubric-anchored, calibration-scored task — the worked_examples block literally carries a 'correct_tier' field, meaning some ratings ARE wrong relative to the rubric.
top_issues.why_it_matters: This is boilerplate lifted from subjective-opinion survey design (satisfaction surveys, UX polls) and is the wrong register for an objective IRR-coding task. It signals to volunteers that careful rubric-matching is optional, which will measurably lower agreement and is the single most likely line a methods-section reviewer would quote back at the authors as evidence the instrument undermines its own construct validity.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Delete the line. Replace with something that keeps volunteers relaxed without denying ground truth exists, e.g.: 'These tiers are defined precisely — do your best to match the rubric rather than a gut feeling, and it's fine to take a moment on the hard ones.'

top_issues.issue: The tier names/numbers are never shown at the point of answering — only in a separate cheat_sheet block read once up front. The response instruction is just 'pick one number, 1-5.'
top_issues.why_it_matters: This forces raters to hold a 5-row, 2-column table in working memory (or scroll back to it) for every single item, which is precisely the re-reading behavior the review brief says must not happen. Per-item response time and error rate both rise the further a rater gets from having last looked at the sheet.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Label the 1-5 response control itself with the short tier names, e.g. buttons/radios reading '1 Public' · '2 Routine' · '3 Internal' · '4 Restricted' · '5 Crown Jewel' (or a persistently pinned/sticky cheat-sheet panel beside every item card). State explicitly in the spec which of these two the final UI uses — it isn't specified here and materially changes the cognitive-load grade.

top_issues.issue: Item cards are not structurally uniform: 4 of 8 cards (vireo-announcements, directory-structure, public-market-data) append an extra parenthetical scoping sentence after 'Choose a number 1-5,' the other 5 do not.
top_issues.why_it_matters: Once a rater has read 2-3 cards without a trailing parenthetical, they build a rhythm of stopping at 'Choose a number 1-5.' A card that then has one more sentence tacked on risks being skipped on a single read — the opposite of the intended effect, since these are the exact items that most need the extra scoping. Format has to be predictable for a one-read form to work.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Either (a) give every card the same fixed final line, e.g. always append a neutral reminder 'Judge only what's described above, at its normal/characteristic use — nothing more, nothing less,' or (b) move all item-specific scoping notes out of the card body into a small fixed micro-label like a 'Scope note:' field that appears in the same visual slot on every card, present or empty, so raters learn where to look for it.

top_issues.issue: estimated_seconds_per_item = 25s is not defensible against the actual per-item reading load: each card has 4 fields (what-it-is, owner, permissions, context) totaling ~60-90 words, plus a mandatory rubric lookup, plus a mandatory public-source-override check, before the rater can commit to a number.
top_issues.why_it_matters: 25s/item covers reading time alone for a short paragraph, not the rubric cross-reference + override check the instructions themselves demand. Undercounting compounds badly over a full item set: at 25s vs a realistic 45-70s, an IRR study sized for e.g. 100 items would be pitched to volunteers as ~40 min but actually run 75-90+ min, which drives late-session fatigue, straight-lining, and dropout — all of which degrade the very agreement statistics the paper reports. The upfront cost of reading instructions + cheat sheet + 4 worked examples (~2-3 min) also isn't accounted for anywhere in the estimate.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Pilot the form with 5-10 people using a stopwatch (not researcher self-estimate), report per-item AND fixed upfront time separately in the paper's methods/appendix, and if total time for the real item count exceeds ~20-25 min, split into multiple shorter sessions or block by server with a break, since ordinal-judgment consistency is known to decay past that point.

top_issues.issue: The plain-instructions summary of the scale ('1 = barely matters ... 5 = emergency the moment it leaks') compresses two independent rubric axes — severity of harm and directness/immediacy of harm — into a single 'how bad' framing.
top_issues.why_it_matters: The actual tier 4 vs 5 boundary in the rubric is not about severity alone, it's specifically about 'one step removed' (4) vs 'no further step needed' (5). Payroll/financials/production data (tier 4) can feel just as severe as live credentials (tier 5) to a rater working only from the one-line summary, since that summary never mentions directness — this is exactly the boundary most likely to produce disagreement, and the top-line instruction (the part most likely to be the only thing read once) doesn't equip raters to make it.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Rewrite the anchor line to carry both axes explicitly, e.g.: 'Rate 1 (nothing left to leak) to 5 (leaking it ALONE is already the emergency, no extra step needed) — severity matters, but so does whether exposure alone does the damage or is one step removed from it.'

top_issues.issue: The 4 worked examples are skewed to the scale's extremes — two are tier 5, one tier 2, one tier 1 — with zero examples at tier 3 or tier 4.
top_issues.why_it_matters: 3 (Internal) vs 4 (Restricted) is the hardest and most consequential boundary in this rubric ('disruptive but recoverable' vs 'serious, lasting harm') and it is also the boundary where most real-world assets in the item set actually cluster (crew rosters, source code, audit logs, project docs). Calibrating raters almost entirely on the unambiguous extremes (live keys vs onboarding docs) leaves the genuinely contested middle of the scale unaddressed, which is where inter-rater disagreement will concentrate and where the paper's IRR numbers are most vulnerable.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Replace one of the two tier-5 examples with a tier-4 example, and add a tier-3 example — ideally a contrastive near-miss pair (e.g., 'internal project roadmap doc' = 3 vs 'signed customer contract' = 4) so raters see exactly where the line falls, not just that it exists.

leading_language_flags: Item 8 (public-market-data): the Context field embeds the rubric's own override sentence almost verbatim — 'a filed Form 4 has nothing left to leak, however sensitive the topic sounds' — which doesn't test whether the rater can apply the public-source override, it just tells them the answer inside the item.

Item 8 also has the parenthetical '(Notice where the data comes FROM, not just the topic it's about.)' stacked on top of the above — two separate nudges toward tier 1 on the single item designed to test the hardest rule in the rubric.

Item 2 (helios-market-bidding-engine): 'the parameters ARE the trading position' (emphasis in source) telegraphs high-tier intent through typographic stress rather than letting the rater infer sensitivity from the facts alone.

Item 4 (vireo-announcements) and item 7 (directory-structure) each carry a scoping parenthetical that pre-resolves the rater's likely objection ('but couldn't this reveal more?') before they can raise it themselves, which risks measuring compliance with the hint rather than independent rubric application.

Item 1 (helios-scada-gateway) and item 5 (aurora-crew-roster) lean on regulatory-label name-dropping ('NERC CIP BES cyber system', 'legal duty-time limits') as the primary sensitivity cue, which nudges toward tier 4/5 via authority-of-regulation rather than via the rubric's actual 'characteristically contains' test.

reviews.persona: A*-venue peer reviewer (IEEE S&P / USENIX Security / CCS caliber) — human-subjects / inter-rater-reliability methodology focus

top_issues.issue: Training-item / test-item leakage: at least three of the eight rated item_cards are near-verbatim restatements of worked_examples that were shown to raters with the answer attached moments earlier. 'security-keys' ('Private key material and certificates ... directly usable to authenticate as the company to outside systems') restates worked_examples[0] ('... directly usable to log in as the company', tier 5). 'vireo-unblinding' ('DSMB coordination and emergency-unblinding request traffic ... reveal which trial subject was unblinded') restates worked_examples[3] almost word-for-word (tier 5). 'public-market-data' restates worked_examples[1] (Form 4 / institutional holdings from an exchange/regulator feed, tier 1).
top_issues.why_it_matters: This is the human-annotation analogue of train/test contamination. Raters aren't exercising independent judgment on these items, they're pattern-matching against an answer key they were handed in the calibration step. Any IRR statistic computed over the full item set will be inflated by these leaked items and will not reflect how raters perform on genuinely unseen material — a reviewer will ask you to report IRR with and without the leaked items and will treat the pooled number as invalid until you do.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Enforce disjointness: worked examples used for training must never reappear (verbatim or near-verbatim) in the scored item pool. Either draft entirely distinct training vignettes, or reserve the four current worked examples as held-out training-only items and replace the three leaked cards with fresh, unseen assets.

top_issues.issue: The 'Context' field on 'public-market-data' quotes the rubric's PUBLIC-DATA OVERRIDE sentence almost verbatim ('Data sourced from an exchange, a regulator, a central bank, a vendor feed, or a news outlet is Public ... however sensitive the topic sounds') and is immediately followed by the coaching parenthetical 'Notice where the data comes FROM, not just the topic it's about.' Similar coaching parentheticals appear on 'vireo-announcements' ('Rate what leaking the CONTENTS would cost, not the separate risk of someone impersonating the channel') and 'directory-structure' ('Judge the names/structure being exposed').
top_issues.why_it_matters: These items no longer measure whether a rater can independently apply an absolute five-tier rubric to an asset description — they measure whether the rater can follow an instruction that is stated on the card itself. That is a construct-validity failure: the instrument is not exercising the judgment it claims to be reliability-testing, and a methods reviewer will say so explicitly.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Strip rule-quoting language and confound-resolution parentheticals from item Context fields. Keep Context purely descriptive (what it is, who owns it, what's allowed, where it's sourced from) and let the rater apply the cheat sheet unaided. If a genuine ambiguity needs resolving for scoring purposes, resolve it in the adjudication protocol, not on the stimulus.

top_issues.issue: No sampling methodology is disclosed: total item-pool size, how these 8 cards (skewed toward tiers 1/2/4/5, with the only tier-3 example living in worked_examples rather than the scored set) were selected from real or synthetic MCP servers, whether selection was random/stratified/adversarial, or how many servers/tools exist in the sampling frame.
top_issues.why_it_matters: A reviewer evaluating sampling strategy will ask directly: is this a representative sample of real MCP-server assets, or a hand-curated set of dramatic edge cases (SCADA/NERC CIP, DSMB unblinding, insider-trading disclosures) built to be cleanly classifiable? The latter threatens external/ecological validity and, combined with the tier skew, means the reliability estimate won't generalize to the messy tier-3 'internal' middle of the scale where most real assets probably sit.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Report the full sampling frame (N servers, N candidate assets), the sampling procedure (e.g., stratified random draw across servers and target tiers), and ensure the scored pool has adequate coverage of all five tiers, not just the extremes. State this in a methods paragraph, ideally pre-registered.

top_issues.issue: No pre-registration of the primary agreement statistic (Krippendorff's alpha with ordinal weighting vs. Fleiss'/Cohen's kappa vs. Gwet's AC1), no pre-specified 'acceptable agreement' threshold, no stated disagreement-adjudication process (third rater? discussion? majority vote?), and no attention-check or gold-item mechanism embedded in the live item stream.
top_issues.why_it_matters: Without a pre-registered analysis plan, a reviewer will assume the statistic was chosen post hoc to produce the most favorable-looking number — a well-known critique of IRR studies at these venues. Absence of an adjudication protocol also means disagreements have no defined resolution, which blocks any downstream 'ground truth' the paper wants to build on.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Pre-register (OSF or equivalent, cited in the paper) the exact statistic, its ordinal/interval weighting scheme for the 1-5 scale, the minimum-N/power justification for the target confidence-interval width, the adjudication procedure for disagreements, and blind gold/attention-check items mixed indistinguishably into the real stream.

top_issues.issue: No blinding or counterbalancing plan for presentation order. Item pairs from the same server (github_helios x2, slack_vireo x2, fs_corp_filesystem x2) appear adjacent in the packet, inviting exactly the kind of cross-asset, within-server comparison the rubric itself forbids ('never relative to the other assets on this server'). There's also no indication that item order, or which items double as worked examples, is randomized/rotated across rater cohorts.
top_issues.why_it_matters: Anchoring and local-consistency effects are a standard threat-to-validity objection: a rater who just scored 'helios-scada-gateway' at tier 4 is primed to score the very next card, from the same server, relative to that judgment rather than against the absolute cheat-sheet anchors — directly undermining the rubric's stated design principle.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Interleave items across servers (never present two same-server cards consecutively), randomize item order per rater with a logged seed, and counterbalance which subset of items each cohort sees as training vs. scored so leakage effects (issue 1) can also be estimated rather than baked in uniformly.

top_issues.issue: No rater-qualification, IRB/consent, or open-materials disclosure. The scored items presuppose cross-domain regulatory fluency (NERC CIP 'BES cyber system' status, ICH-GCP blinding rules, FAA crew duty-time limits, exchange/regulator data-provenance rules) baked directly into the Context field, yet nothing describes who the raters are (security experts? crowdworkers?), how many raters score each item, IRB approval / consent / compensation, or whether the full packet (rubric, cheat sheet, item pool, order-randomization code) will ship as supplementary/artifact material.
top_issues.why_it_matters: This is a human-subjects data-collection instrument; USENIX/CCS/S&P reviewers routinely reject or major-revise papers that omit IRB status and rater-recruitment details, and artifact-evaluation committees will ask for the full instrument and randomization scripts to attempt replication. Separately, if raters are lay annotators, the regulatory context effectively does the tier classification for them (issue 2), meaning the study may be measuring reading comprehension of embedded citations rather than the intended construct.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Add a methods subsection specifying rater count, recruitment/qualification criteria, IRB protocol number and consent process, compensation, and commit to releasing the full annotation packet (rubric text, cheat sheet, item pool with hashes/version, order-randomization code, raw per-rater responses) as a reproducibility artifact.

revised.plain_instructions_md:
You'll see one asset at a time — a data store, channel, or system — described by what it normally contains, who owns it, and what's allowed to happen to it. Rate how bad it would be if THIS asset were exposed, corrupted, or destroyed, using the five-tier scale on your cheat sheet.

Two things decide the tier, not just how sensitive the topic sounds: how severe the harm is, and how DIRECT it is. Rate 1 (nothing left to leak) up to 5 (leaking it ALONE is already the emergency, no extra step needed). A tier-4 asset can feel just as serious as a tier-5 one — the question that separates them is whether exposure alone finishes the harm, or whether something else still has to happen first.

Use the tier definitions on your cheat sheet as the anchor — do not compare an asset to the ones you just rated, and do not compare assets to each other. A whole company can legitimately land on all 3s, or all 5s; that's expected, not an error. Judge what the asset characteristically holds in everyday use, not the worst thing it could theoretically contain.

One override to remember: if the description says data comes from a public source — a stock exchange, a regulator, a news feed — it's tier 1 no matter how sensitive the topic sounds.

Each item's rating control is itself labeled with the short tier names (1 Public/Ephemeral · 2 Routine · 3 Internal · 4 Restricted · 5 Crown Jewel), so you shouldn't need to hold the whole cheat sheet in memory for most items — keep it open beside you anyway for the harder calls, especially telling 3 from 4. Any unfamiliar acronym is defined in place the first time it shows up on a card. A few cards end with a short *Scope note* — read it when it's there; it narrows what you're rating on that one item, it never tells you what number to pick.

These tiers are defined precisely. Do your best to match the rubric rather than a gut feeling — it's fine to take a moment on the harder ones, there's no time pressure to rush past a 3-vs-4 call. Reading these instructions, the cheat sheet, and the worked examples once takes about 3 minutes; after that, most assets go faster than that.

Read the short context paragraph, then pick one number, 1-5, per asset.
revised.tier_cheat_sheet_md:
| # | Tier | One-line rule | Examples |
|---|------|----------------|----------|
| **5** | Crown Jewel | Exposure ALONE is an emergency — no extra step needed | live API keys/credentials, PHI/medical records, money-moving or privileged legal data |
| **4** | Restricted | Serious, lasting harm — but one step removed from the emergency | customer/production data, payroll, financials, proprietary source code, audit logs |
| **3** | Internal | Disruptive/embarrassing, stays in-org, recoverable | project docs, schemas, internal reports, ordinary schedules |
| **2** | Routine | Low value — exposure is a shrug | onboarding material, templates, org charts |
| **1** | Public / Ephemeral | Nothing left to leak, or from a public feed | market quotes, filed financial statements, regulatory disclosures |

**4 vs 5, the key question:** does exposure ALONE finish the harm (5), or does something else still have to happen — a criminal using the data, a lawsuit, a market move — before real damage lands (4)? Both tiers can feel equally serious; directness is what separates them, not severity alone.

**3 vs 4, the key question:** a schedule, document, or log is a 3 by default (ordinary internal material). It only moves to 4 if tampering with it or exposing it would violate a legal/safety limit (e.g., crew duty-time rules) or cause serious, lasting harm to customers or the company's position — not just internal friction.

**Remember:** score what the asset NORMALLY holds • absolute scale, never relative to other assets on this server • public-source data is always 1, regardless of topic.

draft.plain_instructions_md:
For each card, you'll see one tool paired with one type of data or system it can touch. Ask yourself: if this tool is used on this data — normally or through misuse — how far do the effects spread?

Think about how much of that data/system gets touched, and how many people are affected. Do NOT weigh how sensitive or valuable the data is — that's scored elsewhere. Just reach.

Reading something counts the same as changing or deleting it — a full disclosure is just as bad as destruction.

If the tool plainly does nothing to that data or system, choose N/A.

Use the cheat-sheet card to pick a score from 1 (barely touches anything) to 5 (spreads outside the boundary of this data/system entirely, or hits everyone/everything it covers in one shot).

You'll also see the names of the other tools and data types on the same server — use those only to keep your answers consistent with each other, not to change what this specific pair means.

Go with your first honest read. There are no wrong answers here — only your honest judgment.
draft.tier_cheat_sheet_md:
| Score | Name | Rule of thumb |
|---|---|---|
| N/A | Doesn't apply | The tool never touches this data/system |
| 1 | Negligible | One item, at most one person — a pinpoint touch |
| 2 | Minor | A few items, or one small bounded group |
| 3 | Major | Most of it, or several whole sections in one call — big, but still partial |
| 4 | Total, contained | Essentially all of it — but stays inside this data/system's boundary |
| 5 | Systemic | Breaks out — a key/credential is exposed, or it hits every person/item at once, or it's wiped with no way back |

*Reminders:* reading counts the same as changing/deleting. A plain listing of names/metadata is never a 5, no matter how much it covers.

reviews.persona: HCI / survey-design methodologist (IRR form usability review)

top_issues.issue: Split-attention design: the response scale on every item card is bare numbers ("Pick one: N/A · 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5") while the tier definitions live on a separate 'cheat-sheet card'. Raters must hold five tier definitions in working memory or physically flip back to the cheat sheet on every single item.
top_issues.why_it_matters: This is a textbook split-attention effect (Sweller). It defeats the 'one read, no re-reading' goal at the exact moment it matters most — the response action — and multiplies fatigue linearly with item count, since the lookup cost repeats for every card rather than being paid once.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Inline the short tier name next to each number directly in the response prompt on every card, e.g. 'N/A · 1-Negligible · 2-Minor · 3-Major · 4-Total,contained · 5-Systemic', so the decision and the definition are co-located and the separate cheat-sheet card becomes a backup, not a per-item dependency.

top_issues.issue: Several item-card descriptions smuggle sensitivity/value framing into a dimension the rubric explicitly says must price reach only: e.g. 'core grid-control system' (card 1), 'the parameters are the position' (card 2), 'a title alone can reveal an unannounced fleet order or route launch' (card 6), 'a copy lets someone authenticate as us elsewhere' (card 7, paired with a metadata-only tool call).
top_issues.why_it_matters: This risks a halo-effect contamination: raters told 'ignore sensitivity, score only reach' are simultaneously handed prose that emphasizes how important/dangerous the asset is, which is known to inflate severity-adjacent judgments even when instructed not to use it. For an IRR study this is a validity threat, not just a wording nitpick — it can inflate agreement on the wrong basis (shared reaction to stakes) rather than genuine agreement on reach.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Rewrite each card's asset description to state only reach-relevant facts (item/subject counts, scope boundaries, population size — e.g. 'one shared channel, ~40 recipients' instead of 'the traffic reveals which subject was unblinded'). If context on why an asset matters is needed for realism, put it in a clearly-labeled, visually distinct 'context (not scored here)' line separate from the reach facts.

top_issues.issue: The closing line 'There are no wrong answers here — only your honest judgment' directly contradicts the instrument's own design: worked examples carry an explicit 'correct_tier' field, meaning this is scored against a rubric-derived ground truth, not a pure-opinion survey.
top_issues.why_it_matters: Telling careful volunteers there is no wrong answer invites satisficing (lower effort, less re-checking against the cheat sheet) exactly where the study needs maximum care. It also undercuts the credibility of the instructions to a methodologically literate reviewer at submission time, since the paper's own IRR framing assumes a correct-answer rubric.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Replace with calibration language that's honest about the ground truth without inducing anxiety, e.g.: 'Careful readers may land a tier apart on hard cases — that's expected and fine. Apply the rule of thumb as precisely as you can rather than guessing.'

top_issues.issue: The two most counter-intuitive, error-prone rules in the entire rubric — 'disclosure counts the same as destruction' and 'a listing/metadata read is reconnaissance, never a 5' — get the least visual weight: the first is one unbolded clause in paragraph 4 of dense prose; the second appears only as a small italic footnote after the cheat-sheet table.
top_issues.why_it_matters: On a single, non-re-reading pass, salience roughly predicts recall. Burying the rules a rater is MOST likely to get wrong by default intuition (reading feels less bad than deleting; a big listing feels 'systemic') is the opposite of where instructional emphasis should go, and it directly threatens the 'do not differ by more than one tier' consistency goal the rubric states.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Bold both rules in the instructions text, and promote the reconnaissance rule from a footnote into its own labeled row or callout box in the cheat-sheet table itself (e.g. an explicit 'Reconnaissance cap' row), not an easy-to-skip italic postscript.

top_issues.issue: The instruction 'use those [other tools/data on this server] only to keep your answers consistent with each other, not to change what this specific pair means' gives raters a directive they cannot operationalize — no threshold, no worked example, and the rubric's actual consistency rule ('no more than one tier apart without a one-sentence reason') is never stated to them at all.
top_issues.why_it_matters: Vague meta-instructions without an actionable procedure produce inconsistent rater behavior: some will ignore the extra context entirely, others will silently nudge scores toward what they saw on sibling cards, and neither behavior is auditable or reportable in a methods section. It also adds reading load (every card repeats the same 'other tools/other data' boilerplate) for a payoff raters can't act on.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Either drop the 'other tools/data' block from the per-item cards entirely (move it to a persistent, non-repeated server-level sidebar), or replace the vague sentence with the actual operational rule from the rubric: 'If this same kind of call scores more than one tier apart on two similar assets, jot a one-sentence reason why.'

top_issues.issue: The estimated_seconds_per_item of 25s does not match the actual reading load: cards average ~90-130 words including domain jargon a general volunteer won't have on-hand (SCADA, DSMB unblinding, freebusy, usergroups, wholesale settlement), and the ~230-word instructions plus table plus 4 worked examples (~5 minutes of onboarding) aren't budgeted anywhere.
top_issues.why_it_matters: An unrealistic per-item time estimate in the paper's methods section is a concrete point a reviewer will challenge (self-reported vs. measured completion time is a common IRR-study critique), and it also risks under-resourcing volunteers in practice — leading to rushed, lower-quality first passes that undermine the very IRR numbers being collected.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Pilot the actual form with 2-3 naive volunteers, log wall-clock time per item including the first-item ramp-up, and report a measured (not assumed) per-item time with a separate onboarding-time line, rather than a single flat 25s figure.

Card 5 (usergroups_users_update / vireo-announcements): 'already seen by everyone, so only spoofing matters' pre-interprets the judgment for the rater rather than describing the population/scope.

Card 7 (get_file_info / security-keys): 'a copy lets someone authenticate as us elsewhere' primes an escape/5 reading even though this specific tool call returns metadata only (size, timestamps, permissions), not key contents — a mismatch between the framing and what the call actually does.
Card 1 (get_file_contents / helios-scada-gateway): 'core grid-control system' is stakes/value framing on a card meant to be scored on reach alone.
Card 2 (get_file_contents / helios-market-bidding-engine): 'the parameters are the position' is sensitivity framing, not a reach fact.

reviews.persona: A*-venue peer reviewer (IEEE S&P / USENIX Security / CCS caliber) — human-subjects security-taxonomy annotation methodology
leading_language_flags: "one call crosses the whole estate" (card 3, search_code/code-records) states the reach conclusion directly in the stimulus instead of describing the mechanism, pre-empting the tier-4/5 judgment.
"already seen by everyone, so only spoofing matters" (card 5, usergroups_users_update/vireo-announcements) hands the rater the answer's reasoning verbatim.

"a copy lets someone authenticate as us elsewhere" (card 7, get_file_info/security-keys) echoes the rubric's own tier-5 'escape' definition almost word-for-word, despite the tool returning metadata only — directly conflicts with the rubric's 'metadata is never an escape' rule.
"no read, search, or quoting, by anyone, ever" (card 4) frames a policy prohibition as an absolute, reading as a severity signal rather than a reach fact.
"a title alone can reveal an unannounced fleet order or route launch" (card 6) injects sensitivity/impact language into a reach-only card.
"the parameters are the position" (card 2) imports value/stakes framing that belongs to the separately-scored sensitivity dimension.
"a core grid-control system" (card 1) leads with criticality framing rather than reach-relevant facts (item count, subject count).
"Default classification: Public" (card 8) imports a sensitivity-tier label into a card meant to isolate reach only.

top_issues.issue: Item card 7 (get_file_info on security-keys) violates the rubric it is supposed to implement.
top_issues.why_it_matters: The rubric explicitly says reading a listing/metadata is reconnaissance and 'never an escape' (tier 5 is reserved for cases like a full key read that unlocks another system). But get_file_info returns only size/timestamps/permissions/type — no key contents — while the card's asset text ('a copy lets someone authenticate as us elsewhere') supplies the exact tier-5 escape rationale from the rubric itself. This primes raters toward 5 for a call the rubric requires to be low, which will either (a) manufacture spurious disagreement between rubric-literal raters (1–2) and prompt-primed raters (5), deflating measured IRR for reasons that have nothing to do with the construct, or (b) if this is an intentional 'trap/compliance' item, it is undisclosed as such and will silently distort the primary agreement statistic if pooled with ordinary items. A reviewer will ask which of these it is and why it wasn't caught in piloting.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Rewrite the card to describe only what get_file_info actually returns (metadata fields, count of items touched, subject count) and move the 'authenticates elsewhere' escape rationale to wherever the sensitivity/value dimension is scored. If a rubric-compliance probe is wanted, tag it explicitly in the item bank and exclude it from the primary kappa/alpha, reporting it separately as a manipulation check.

top_issues.issue: Reach cards are contaminated with sensitivity/value language the task explicitly says is out of scope.
top_issues.why_it_matters: The instructions state 'Do NOT weigh how sensitive or valuable the data is — that's scored elsewhere. Just reach,' and the rubric header says 'value is priced separately.' Yet cards 1, 2, 4, 6, and 8 all embed criticality/value adjectives ('core grid-control system,' 'the parameters are the position,' unblinding/DSMB framing, 'unannounced fleet order,' 'Default classification: Public'). This creates a discriminant-validity confound: the study cannot claim Blast Radius and Sensitivity are measured independently if the Blast Radius stimulus itself carries sensitivity cues. This is a first-order construct-validity objection in any methods section claiming the two dimensions are orthogonal.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Strip all value/impact adjectives from card text; state only mechanical, reach-relevant facts (how many items/subjects the call can touch, whether the tool acts on the asset at all). Move domain color needed for comprehension into a separate glossary the rater can consult, not into the scored stimulus.

top_issues.issue: No total item count (N), sampling frame, or sampling method is specified for the actual instrument — only 8 illustrative cards are shown with no indication of how they were drawn from the full catalog of tool×asset pairs across all servers.
top_issues.why_it_matters: For Krippendorff's alpha or weighted kappa, the confidence interval on the reliability estimate itself depends on N and its distribution across tiers (including a deliberate share of N/A and boundary cases). Without a stated N, stratification (by server, by expected tier, by tool category), and a precision/power justification, a reviewer cannot tell whether a reported IRR reflects the instrument or reflects noise from a small, possibly cherry-picked set of clear-cut items — the 8 shown here look hand-selected for maximal clarity rather than representative of ambiguous real cases.
top_issues.concrete_fix: State total N of scored pairs, describe a stratified or random sampling procedure across all servers and expected tiers (with a floor quota of N/A and boundary items), and report a target CI half-width for the primary agreement statistic in a pre-registration.

top_issues.issue: The analysis plan is not pre-specified: it is unclear whether the target quantity is rater–rater agreement or rater-vs-gold accuracy against the 'correct_tier' labels shown in worked examples, and how the structurally distinct N/A category is weighted against the ordinal 1–5 scale.
top_issues.why_it_matters: Mixing a nominal/nonapplicable category into an ordinal weighting scheme (e.g., quadratic-weighted kappa or Krippendorff's alpha with an interval/ordinal difference function) is a well-known source of arbitrary, hard-to-defend results depending on how N/A is coded. If gold labels exist (as implied by 'correct_tier' in worked examples), the study may actually be measuring accuracy against a criterion, not pure IRR — these require different statistics, different reporting, and different claims. Reviewers will ask for the exact statistic, the N/A weighting scheme, the adjudication protocol for ties, and confirmation the rubric was locked before data collection (not iteratively patched based on early disagreement, which would make the final IRR number circular).
top_issues.concrete_fix: Pre-register (e.g., OSF) the exact statistic and its N/A-handling rule, the disagreement-adjudication procedure, and a rubric freeze date; report any post-freeze rubric edits as an explicit amendment with before/after IRR numbers.

top_issues.issue: Calibration/independence contamination: raters are shown 'the names of the other tools and data types on the same server ... to keep your answers consistent,' and the four worked examples are structurally near-identical to specific item cards (same servers, overlapping or adjacent asset names, matching rhetorical templates, e.g. worked example 3's 'one call returns every path on the entire share → 4' mirrors item card 3's 'one call crosses the whole estate').
top_issues.why_it_matters: This is a deliberate non-independence instruction with no manipulation check attached, plus likely calibration-set leakage into the scored set. A reviewer cannot distinguish 'raters agree because they understand the rubric' from 'raters agree because they pattern-matched the worked example's phrasing to a similarly-worded item.' Since IRR is the paper's headline methodological claim, this ambiguity alone is reviewer-fatal without a mitigation.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Either remove the 'other tools/data on this server' context entirely (score each pair in isolation, the standard for independence) or run it as an explicit between-subjects manipulation and report its effect on agreement. Separately, audit and report zero overlap in asset/tool naming and rhetorical structure between the worked-example set and the scored item set, or justify any overlap explicitly.

top_issues.issue: No stated instrument-level reproducibility artifacts: rater count/recruitment/expertise, IRB/ethics approval, pilot-testing of the rubric before the full run, and no fatigue/attention-check plan despite an unspecified but likely large total item count.
top_issues.why_it_matters: A*-venue human-subjects security papers routinely get desk-rejected or majorly revised for missing basics: who the annotators were (security experts vs. crowdworkers changes the entire interpretation of the IRR number), whether the protocol was IRB-approved or exempt, whether the instrument was piloted before the reported run, and how fatigue/attention were controlled over a session whose total length isn't even computable from the draft since N is unspecified.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Add a methods appendix specifying rater recruitment and expertise criteria, IRB status, a documented pilot phase with its own (smaller) IRR check before the full run, embedded attention-check items with a pre-registered exclusion rule, and a stated total item count with expected session length and break points.

top_issues.issue: Card 3 (search_code / code-records) states "Normal use: none — one call crosses the whole estate," which nearly restates the tier-4 rubric text ("essentially everything the asset holds... in one call"). This tells raters the intended answer's magnitude in the rubric's own vocabulary rather than letting them infer it from a neutral operational description.
top_issues.why_it_matters: A card that echoes the tier definition's phrasing back at the rater manufactures artificial rater agreement — the IRR statistic will look strong not because raters share understanding of the construct, but because the item told them the answer. This specifically undermines the paper's core claim (agreement reflects genuine construct validity).
top_issues.concrete_fix: Rewrite the 'Used on' line to a neutral operational fact only, e.g. "search_code returns matching snippets from every repository the caller has read access to." Drop "crosses the whole estate" and any other phrase that paraphrases a tier label.

top_issues.issue: Card 7 (get_file_info / security-keys) reads: "a copy lets someone authenticate as us elsewhere" — this is almost verbatim the rubric's own tier-5 trigger language ("a credential/key that unlocks another system"). But get_file_info's own tool description says it returns metadata only, no contents, and the rubric's explicit RULE says metadata/listing reads are reconnaissance and 'never an escape.' The card therefore primes raters toward 5 while the rubric, correctly applied, caps this well below 5.
top_issues.why_it_matters: This is simultaneously a leading-language problem and a technical-correctness problem: the intended answer per the RULE is a low tier (metadata read = pinpoint recon), but the vivid escape-language in the description will likely pull most raters to 5 regardless of what the tool actually returns. If this is meant to be the calibration item testing whether raters apply the metadata exception, the description defeats its own purpose by over-supplying tier-5 vocabulary right next to a metadata-only tool.

A security-domain rater who knows the Slack Admin API will notice the tool cannot do what the card implies, lose confidence in the instrument, and either mark N/A (technically correct, since the tool never touches this asset) or guess at what the designers intended — both outcomes inject noise unrelated to genuine rubric disagreement, and in a published IRR study this kind of item-level error is exactly what a reviewer would find on inspection and use to question the whole item bank's quality control.

top_issues.issue: The unexplained "Normal use: ..." field appears on 6 of 8 cards (1,2,3,4,5,7) with consistently absolutist prohibition language ("no role has source access here," "no read, search, or quoting, by anyone, ever," "no sanctioned workflow touches key material") and is silently absent on cards 6 and 8. Nothing in plain_instructions_md tells raters what this field is for or that it should NOT influence the reach score.
top_issues.why_it_matters: Blast Radius is explicitly reach-only; permission/governance context is a value-adjacent signal that belongs to a different dimension. Because every 'Normal use: none' card in this set also happens to be a higher-stakes asset, raters can learn the shortcut 'forbidden phrasing → score higher' without ever reasoning about actual reach — this is a systemic leaking pattern across the whole card set, not a single wording slip, and it directly undermines the paper's separation of reach from value/sensitivity that the rubric is designed to test.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Either delete the 'Normal use' line from all Blast-Radius cards (it isn't needed to answer reach), or if it must stay for shared-card-format reasons with another dimension, add one explicit sentence to plain_instructions_md: "The 'Normal use' note is policy context only — it does not change this score." Also make the field's presence consistent across all cards (add or remove) so its presence/absence doesn't itself become a cue.

top_issues.issue: Cards 1 and 2 both use `get_file_contents`, whose own tool description is "get the contents of a file OR DIRECTORY" — an ambiguous unit of reach. Neither card states whether the call fetches one file or an entire directory tree, so the same tool could plausibly justify tier 1 (one file, pinpoint) or tier 2/3 (a directory's worth of files) depending on an assumption the card never states.
top_issues.why_it_matters: This pair is clearly designed as the study's built-in consistency check (rubric rule: 'the same kind of call on two comparable assets should not differ by more than one tier without a one-sentence reason'). If the call's scope is left ambiguous, different raters will silently assume different scopes and disagree for a reason that has nothing to do with true rubric interpretation — contaminating exactly the pair meant to test cross-asset consistency.
top_issues.concrete_fix: State the concrete call shape explicitly, matching the specificity already used correctly in the directory_tree worked example, e.g. "reading one named source file from the repository" (if tier 1 is intended) or "recursively fetching every file under the repository root" (if a broader tier is intended).

Over a trial's lifetime, an emergency-unblinding channel's history plausibly contains many past unblinding requests for many different subjects, not one.
top_issues.why_it_matters: If the intended answer is tier 1 ('one subject at most'), the card's own tool semantics contradict it — a full-history fetch is a multi-subject disclosure, which by the rubric's own reach ladder is closer to tier 2 ('a few items/subjects') or higher depending on trial size. A domain reviewer will flag this as the description not matching what the API call actually returns, which is a correctness defect independent of any leading-language concern.
top_issues.concrete_fix: Either scope the described call explicitly ("fetching the most recent unblinding request" for tier 1) or, if it genuinely returns full history, revise the description to acknowledge multiple past subjects are included and adjust the intended tier accordingly.

reviews.persona: Novice rater — no security/InfoSec background, encountering this form cold (first-time annotator)

top_issues.issue: Some cards don't establish that the tool actually touches the named asset, leaving me to guess between N/A and some positive tier.
top_issues.why_it_matters: Item 5 pairs usergroups_users_update (a tool that edits a user-group member list) with vireo-announcements (a broadcast channel) — the card never explains the mechanism connecting the two (does editing the group change who can post to the channel? who's auto-subscribed?). top_issues.issue: The flat 25-second-per-item estimate doesn't match the actual reading load, and the draft never states the total number of cards a rater will face.
top_issues.why_it_matters: Just reading the instructions, cheat-sheet, and 4 worked examples carefully took me several minutes before touching a single card, and cards with jargon or ambiguous mechanism (items 2, 5, 6, 7, 8 above) each took well over a minute once I tried to actually reason rather than pattern-match. 25 sec/item is only plausible after heavy practice on unambiguous cards; for a first-timer it will run 2-4x that on a meaningful fraction of items, and the paper will need an honest per-item time distribution (not a flat assumption) to justify rater burden and any time-based exclusion criteria.

top_issues.issue: Item 6's scope is genuinely ambiguous between a tier-2 and a tier-5 answer, and the card doesn't resolve it.

Item 4 (conversations_history/vireo-unblinding): 'no read, search, or quoting, by anyone, ever' — policy-prohibition intensity, not reach, but reads as a strong hint to score high.
